---
title: "Predictive modeling of claims status"
author: 'Miles Reynolds, Sid Revanuru, Iris Li, Aaron, Makala Mesina-Forester'
date: today
---

### Abstract

The input data used for training the models were header and paragraph content scraped from webpages. We vectorized the data using term frequencies of the word tokens to turn the string data into numeric data, required for training. Additional feature reduction using PCA was conducted to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. For binary class predictions of the provided testing set, a support vector machine was used, while, for multiclass predictions, a multiclass logistic regression model was used. Testing the models against a heldout test set, the support machine resulted in an accuracy of 80.1%. The multiclass logistic regression yielded an accuracy of 79.9%.

### Preprocessing

Following preliminary task 1, the preprocessing pipeline first involved extracting the (<p>) and header content (<h>) from the HTML files. The raw content text were then cleaned by imputing missing values and using TF-IDF vectorization to turn the corpus into quantitative values, separating them by bigrams after considering the results of task 2. The response variables were also encoded using a LabelEncoder() to turn the string values into numeric values. Following that, we reduced the dimensionality of the feature space by using PCA.

### Methods

For binary classification, we compared three models on the same TF-IDF features: logistic regression, linear support vector machine (SVM), and naive Bayes models. The regularization strengths (C = 10 for logistic regression, C = 1 for the SVM) were taken from an earlier 5-fold grid search over C (logistic regression: 1, 10, 100; SVM: 0.1, 1, 10), and naive Bayes used default settings. The data was split 80/20, stratified by class. The models were compared with 10-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set.

For multi-class classification, we compared model results between a multiclass logistic regression model and a neural network model following the conclusions derived from the preliminary tasks. Upon hyperparameter tuning and comparing the AUC and accuracy scores, we ended up using a multiclass logistic regression model with an elastic net penalty. The resulting parameters for the elastic net penalty were `l1_ratio` = 0.22 and `C` = 0.5. They were selected using a grid search cross-validation technique that performed cross-validation across different combinations of the hyperparameters. The training and testing split used was 80/20 with 5 layers of cross-validation.

### Results

For binary classification models, the linear support vector machine SVM has the highest accuracy (80.1%, versus 79.4% for logistic regression and 76.2% for naive Bayes).

For multiclass classification, the multiclass logistic regression with `l1_ratio` = 0.22 and `C` = 0.5 had the highest accuracy (79.9%, versus 79.6% for a neural network).

Results of the models (binary and multiclass) tested against a holdout testing set are shown below:

|             | Binary (SVM) | Multiclass (Logistic Regression) |
|-------------|--------------|----------------------------------|
| Sensitivity | 0.813        | 0.689                            |
| Specificity | 0.788        | 0.934                            |
| Accuracy    | 0.801        | 0.799                            |
| AUC         | 0.874        | 0.940                            |
